pillar: Brain Tumour Treatment: Advanced Options and Global Access

items.q: Is Beijing Tiantan Hospital a good choice for brain tumour (glioma) surgery?
items.a: Beijing Tiantan Hospital is a strong option for glioma and other brain tumour surgery, performing more than 10,000 neurosurgical procedures a year with awake craniotomy, intraoperative MRI-guided resection, and 5-ALA fluorescence-guided techniques available for eligible cases. The hospital's neuro-oncology multidisciplinary tumour board reviews international patient imaging and pathology before confirming a surgical plan, and Gamma Knife ICON radiosurgery is available for brain metastases, meningioma, and other lesions suited to non-invasive treatment. Whether surgery, radiosurgery, or a combined approach is appropriate depends on tumour type, location, grade, and prior treatment, and should be confirmed through specialist review of your specific imaging and pathology before any travel decision is made.

items.q: What is carbon ion therapy, and is it available for brain tumours in China?
items.a: Carbon ion therapy is a high-precision radiation technique with greater biological effectiveness than conventional radiation or even proton therapy, and it is available in China at the Shanghai Proton and Heavy Ion Center (SPHIC) — one of only around 15 centres offering it worldwide. SPHIC uses carbon ion therapy for radioresistant brain tumours such as glioblastoma (GBM), chordoma, and skull base tumours, often for patients whose tumours have recurred after prior radiation. Standard proton therapy is also offered at SPHIC for low-grade glioma, paediatric tumours, and pituitary tumours. Suitability for carbon ion or proton therapy depends on tumour type, location, prior treatment, and specialist review of imaging by the treating radiation oncology team.

items.q: How much does brain tumour surgery cost in China compared to the USA and Europe?
items.a: Brain tumour surgery such as craniotomy with intraoperative MRI and 5-ALA guidance costs an estimated $8,000–18,000 at Beijing Tiantan Hospital in China, compared to roughly $50,000–120,000 in the USA and $35,000–70,000 in Germany or Switzerland for a broadly comparable procedure. These are estimated ranges only; the exact cost for any patient depends on tumour complexity, length of hospital stay, additional diagnostics, and the specific surgical protocol recommended after specialist review of imaging and pathology. A centre-specific cost estimate can be provided once your reports have been reviewed, but final pricing is confirmed directly by the treating hospital.

items.q: How much does carbon ion therapy at SPHIC cost compared to Japan and Germany?
items.a: A full course of carbon ion therapy for a brain tumour at SPHIC in Shanghai is estimated at $50,000–80,000, compared to roughly $80,000–130,000 in Japan and $90,000–140,000 at Heidelberg's carbon ion centre in Germany. These figures are estimated ranges rather than fixed quotes, since the number of treatment sessions, imaging requirements, and length of stay vary by tumour type and treatment protocol. Final costs are confirmed by SPHIC after case review, and patients should treat any published figure as a planning estimate rather than a guaranteed price, discussing the specifics with their oncology team before committing to travel.

items.q: How long do I need to stay in China for proton or carbon ion therapy at SPHIC?
items.a: Most patients travelling to SPHIC in Shanghai for proton or carbon ion brain tumour therapy should plan for a 4–8 week on-site stay, depending on the treatment protocol and number of fractions prescribed by the radiation oncology team. This period covers initial planning scans, the full course of daily treatment sessions, and any interim imaging review. The exact duration depends on tumour type, treatment technique, and individual response, and is confirmed by SPHIC's multidisciplinary team once a patient's case has been reviewed; accommodation and interpreter support for the full stay can be arranged separately.

items.q: Can a child with a brain tumour be treated at SPHIC's particle therapy programme?
items.a: Yes, children with brain tumours such as medulloblastoma, ependymoma, or low-grade glioma may be considered for SPHIC's dedicated paediatric particle therapy programme in Shanghai, which uses proton therapy to reduce radiation exposure to surrounding healthy brain tissue. Paediatric cases are reviewed by a multidisciplinary team that includes neuroradiation oncology and neurosurgery specialists before a treatment plan is confirmed. Eligibility depends on the child's specific diagnosis, tumour location, prior treatment, and overall health, and should be discussed with a qualified paediatric oncology team alongside SPHIC's specialists before any travel is arranged.

items.q: Is carbon ion therapy an option if my brain tumour has already been treated with radiation before?
items.a: Carbon ion re-irradiation at SPHIC may be considered for select patients whose brain tumour, such as glioblastoma, has recurred after previous radiation therapy, since carbon ion beams can be delivered with a different biological profile than conventional re-treatment. SPHIC is one of the few centres worldwide offering carbon ion retreatment for recurrent post-radiotherapy brain tumours, which is a significant draw for patients who have exhausted standard options elsewhere. Whether re-irradiation is appropriate depends on the original radiation dose received, time since prior treatment, tumour location, and a detailed review of imaging by SPHIC's radiation oncology team — this decision should always involve the patient's existing oncology team as well.

items.q: What molecular and genetic tests are performed on brain tumour tissue at Tiantan Hospital?
items.a: Beijing Tiantan Hospital performs full molecular and genetic testing on brain tumour tissue, including next-generation sequencing (NGS), IDH mutation status, MGMT methylation, 1p/19q co-deletion, TERT promoter mutation, H3K27M mutation, and CDKN2A status — the panel used to classify gliomas under current diagnostic criteria. If a patient's home-country pathology report is incomplete, tumour tissue blocks can be sent to Tiantan for re-testing before a treatment plan is finalized. These results directly influence whether surgery, radiotherapy, particle therapy, or a clinical trial is the most appropriate next step, and should be reviewed together with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Can I get a specialist second opinion from Tiantan or SPHIC before travelling to China?
items.a: Yes, patients can obtain a specialist second opinion from Tiantan or SPHIC's neuro-oncology teams through a remote telemedicine consultation before deciding whether to travel to China. After medical records, imaging, and pathology are reviewed, an online consultation is arranged with the treating neurosurgeon or radiation oncologist, with simultaneous medical interpretation, resulting in a written treatment plan and cost estimate. This lets patients and their home oncology team evaluate the recommendation before committing to travel. A second opinion does not obligate a patient to proceed with treatment in China, and any final decision should be made jointly with the patient's existing medical team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients access brain tumour treatment at Tiantan or SPHIC?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or trials, estimate costs, and coordinate travel, visa, and follow-up support alongside the treating oncology team. For brain tumour patients considering Tiantan or SPHIC, this includes reviewing imaging and pathology against each centre's eligibility criteria, arranging telemedicine consultations, securing the medical visa invitation letter, providing on-ground interpreters throughout treatment, and coordinating post-treatment follow-up with the patient's home oncologist. CancerFax does not replace the treating physician — all treatment decisions remain with the patient's oncology team.
